entry.title: America's Longest Siege: Siege of Port Hudson 1863

media:group.media:title: America's Longest Siege: Siege of Port Hudson 1863
media:group.media:description:
Thank you to Fatal Frontier 1869 for sponsoring this video. Try it today for free on PC! http://bit.ly/4dDXLhJ
While Grant is rapidly marching upon the Confederate river bastion of Vicksburg. Another Federal Army marches upon its little sister, Port Hudson. Major General Nathaniel P. Banks, a disgraced political general from the Eastern Theater, was sent to Louisiana in December of 1862 to take over command of the Department of the Gulf from its previous commander, Major General Benjamin Butler. Lincoln dispatched Banks to work with Grant to destroy the final rebel holdouts along the Mississippi River. Therefore, in May of 1863, following reports that the Port Hudson commander, Major General Franklin K. Gardner, had sent half his garrison to support Pemberton, Banks rapidly moved his massive XIX Corps to quickly take out the Louisiana stronghold. However, despite having fewer than 7,000 men, Gardner's defenders had chosen a highly defensible position to garrison. Regardless, knowing that Port Hudson only contains a small garrison, Banks expects a swift victory. Thus, Banks launches his massive corps against the tiny rebel garrison on May 27th, 1863, starting the siege of Port Hudson.

entry.title: Grant's Masterpiece: The Vicksburg Campaign 1862-63 (All Parts)

media:group.media:title: Grant's Masterpiece: The Vicksburg Campaign 1862-63 (All Parts)
media:group.media:description:
In the winter of 1862, Major General Ulysses S. Grant launches his bold Vicksburg Campaign, marching the Army of the Tennessee south from Tennessee along the Mississippi Central Railroad to seize the Confederate stronghold controlling the Mississippi River. But before the Illinois general can get far, disaster strikes when Major General Earl Van Dorn destroys his supply base at Holly Springs in a daring cavalry raid. Without supplies in the middle of enemy country in the dead of winter, Grant has no other choice but to retreat. Simultaneously, William T. Sherman’s riverborne assault meets fierce resistance and is bloodily repulsed at the Battle of Chickasaw Bayou.
Undeterred, Grant pivots his army to the Mississippi River. Unable to cut his way through the swamps of Northeastern Louisiana in early 1863, Grant and Porter devise a plan to run the daunting Vicksburg that overlooks the De Soto Peninsula and the bend in the river. On the night of April 16, 1863, Porter’s gunboats and transports run the gauntlet of Vicksburg’s formidable river batteries, emerging battered but intact south of the city. With federal ships in the gap between the rebel bastions of Vicksburg and Port Hudson, Grant crosses the Mississippi on April 30. Grant's crossing of the Mississippi is the largest amphibious landing in American history to that date.
Living off the land, Grant and his army quickly marches inland, defeats multiple rebel forces, cuts the vital Mississippi Central Railroad, and captures Jackson, the state capital. Following the capture of Jackson, Grant pivots his army west towards Vicksburg. As the Federals march, they come into contact with Lieutenant General John C. Pemberton's Army of Mississippi at Champion Hill. On May 16, the two sides come to blows on the Champion Plantation. However, with the Federals heavily outnumbering the Confederates, Grant easily shatters Pemberton's rebels. Unable to stop Grant, Pemberton falls back into Vicksburg’s defenses. The following day, Grant invests the city and begins the pivotal Siege of Vicksburg. After multiple attacks, two explosions, and nearly two months of skirmishing, Pemberton surrenders on July 4, 1863. With the Capture of Vicksburg, Grant splits the Confederacy in two and secures Union control of the Mississippi for the remainder of the American Civil War.

After crushing Pemberton at the Battles of Champion Hill and Big Black River Bridge, Major General Ulysses S. Grant drives his Army of Tennessee across the Big Black towards the city that has, since the beginning of the war, thwarted every attempt to be captured by the Federals: Vicksburg. Once near the outskirts of Vicksburg, Grant prepares his men to assault the extensive earthworks the rebels have been constructing. Meanwhile, inside the threatened city, Pemberton, who watched his defeated Army of Mississippi be herded into the river bastion following their two crushing defeats, anxiously waits for Grant's blue horde to assail his position. With General Joseph E. Johnston gathering a relief army only 60 miles away in Canton. Both commanders know if Grant wants to take Vicksburg, he will have to attack and attack soon. Therefore, during the next month, Grant will do whatever it takes to break into one of the most heavily fortified bastions on the North American Continent.

entry.title: Hellfire on the Mississippi: Running the Vicksburg Batteries 1863

media:group.media:title: Hellfire on the Mississippi: Running the Vicksburg Batteries 1863
media:group.media:description:
Following his failure to take Vicksburg in the final months of 1862. Major General Ulysses S. Grant decides to pivot his Army of the Tennessee to the Mississippi River. Grant hopes that, with his cooperation with Rear Admiral David D. Porter's Mississippi Squadron, he can find a way to bypass the stubborn Confederate defenses that are preventing him from reaching Vicksburg's rear. To do this, Grant sets his subordinates to work on different projects, from building canals, blowing up dams, to finding hidden bayous to outflank the rebel earthworks. If his schemes ultimately do not pan out, Grant's last option is to outflank the city altogether and march upon it from the south. But before he can do this, he will need federal ships in the Confederate wedge between Vicksburg and its sister, Port Hudson. However, that will require the risky venture of running the daunting guns that infest the bluffs of Vicksburg....

On April 27, 1863, once his army is ready, Hooker secretly sends out the V, XI, and XII Corps on a march around Lee's left flank, bound for the exposed Confederate rear. For the first 36 hours, Lee is completely unaware of what is happening just across the Rappahannock. At the same time, Hooker initiates the other part of his plan and sends Sedgwick's VI Corps across the river just south of Fredericksburg. It is not until May 30 that the Confederate general gets the first reports of a federal column marching into his rear. Unsure of its size or intention, Lee leaves a small force to hold Sedgwick and sends Jackson with the rest of his Second Corps west against this unknown column. The next day, the two forces will come to blows in the dense woods of the Virginia Wilderness, near the forest manor of Chancellorsville.

Following the disastrous Battle of Fredericksburg, the Army of the Potomac's morale sinks to its lowest point ever. Burnside, witnessing the wretched state his men are in, tries to rectify the situation by sending his men on another campaign in the midst of winter. However, his men are caught in a freezing cold storm that turns the roads to mud. Unable to power through this deluge, Burnside recalls his men in disgrace. Realizing there is nothing more he can do, Burnside forces Lincoln to accept his resignation from army command and is replaced by the one man he despises, Joseph Hooker. Hooker, seeing how horribly Burnside let the condition of the army fall, jumps into action to get it back into fighting shape. While the Federals are working on themselves, Lee begins planning his next invasion into the north, but before he can advance north into Maryland, he'll need food, more food than his supply lines can bring. Forcing Lee to look for untouched places across the commonwealth to procure his much-needed resources.

entry.title: Yanks Invade Texas: Battle of Galveston 1863

media:group.media:title: Yanks Invade Texas: Battle of Galveston 1863
media:group.media:description:
Following the capture of the premier port city in Texas in October of 1862, the Confederates left believe it will only be a matter of time before the Federals push deeper into the Lone Star State. Sensing the crisis building in the Trans-Mississippi, President Jefferson Davis dispatches Maj. Gen. John B. Magruder to Texas to retake the city before the Federals become fully entrenched. Yet, unlike the eastern Confederacy, Texas lacks the fundamental resources to wage a proper war against the invaders. This predicament forces Magruder to be creative and scourge for anything he can get his hands on. However, he cannot wait long, as the longer he dallies, the longer the Federals have to reinforce and further entrench themselves on the island. Thus, unable to waste much time, Magruder will have to take his chances and go all in with a single, desperate assault to reclaim the island city of Galveston for the Confederacy.

entry.title: Stones River Campaign: Rosecrans Takes Command

media:group.media:title: Stones River Campaign: Rosecrans Takes Command
media:group.media:description:
Following the failure of Bragg's Invasion of Kentucky. The Confederate Army of Mississippi returned to Tennessee in chaos. Two sides sprang up in the army, one side was with Bragg, and the other was against Bragg. This verbal conflict was so great that the Confederate president himself, Jefferson Davis, was forced to intervene to ensure that the army would not crumble. Meanwhile, in the Federal Army of the Ohio, similar chaos ensued as many prominent officials called for the ousting of Buell, who had failed to command his army effectively during Bragg's invasion of the Bluegrass State. Major General William S. Rosecrans, who won solid victories in Mississippi, was chosen to command in Buell's stead. As both armies face reorganizations, Middle Tennessee beckons for both sides to fill the void. In the last few months of 1862, both Bragg and Rosecrans will pivot their armies, hoping to take or protect the volunteer state's capital, Nashville.

entry.title: Sherman's Bloody Bayou: Battle of Chickasaw Bayou 1862

media:group.media:title: Sherman's Bloody Bayou: Battle of Chickasaw Bayou 1862
media:group.media:description:
Following the defeat of Van Dorn's desperate attack upon Corinth in early October. Major General Ulysses S. Grant directs his forces against his next target, the annoying river citadel of Vicksburg, Mississippi. Once all his forces are ready, Grant unleashes his Army of the Tennessee south down the Mississippi Central Railroad in early December. Facing this threat is newly promoted Lieutenant General John C Pemberton. With only half the numbers Grant has, Pemberton barrages Richmond for more men and supplies. Yet, while he faces an overland threat coming from Tennessee, a new, dangerous threat is forming on the mighty Mississippi. While Grant pushes his army south, Major General John A. McClernand is assembling a naval force to strike the city via the Mississippi. As the end of 1862 grows ever nearer, Pemberton faces a two-pronged advance from both land and river. A crisis that no other Confederate officer is facing in the closing months of 1862.
